record.original_question: A finite latticeLhasnjoin-irreducibles. What is the most numberf(n) of meet-irreducible elementsLcan have?

evidence.quote: [Stan2012, Ch. 3 Exer. 29] A finite latticeLhasnjoin-irreducibles. What is the most numberf(n) of meet-irreducible elementsLcan have?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $L$ be a finite lattice. An element $x \in L$ is called join-irreducible if $x$ is not the minimum element of $L$ and whenever $x = a \vee b$ for some $a,b \in L$, one has $x = a$ or $x = b$. Dually, $x \in L$ is called meet-irreducible if $x$ is not the maximum element of $L$ and whenever $x = a \wedge b$ for some $a,b \in L$, one has $x = a$ or $x = b$.

For a positive integer $n$, define
$$f(n) = \max\{\,m\,:\,\text{there exists a finite lattice } L \text{ with exactly } n \text{ join-irreducibles and exactly } m \text{ meet-irreducibles}\,\}.$$

Determine $f(n)$ (or, more generally, determine the asymptotic behavior of $f(n)$ as $n \to \infty$).
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is listed as a long-standing open problem in Stanley's Enumerative Combinatorics (Vol. 1, Chapter 3, Exercise 29) and reappears in recent compilations of open problems on tableau/poset combinatorics. No closed-form expression or tight asymptotic for f(n) appears to be known; only loose upper and lower bounds are available in the literature on finite lattices.

status_evidence.title: Enumerative Combinatorics Volume 1 (Stanley)
status_evidence.snippet: Chapter 3 Exercise 29 asks for the maximum number f(n) of meet-irreducibles in a finite lattice with n join-irreducibles.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as a research-level exercise in Stanley's textbook with no known solution.

status_evidence.title: On generation of finite posets by meet-irreducibles
status_evidence.snippet: Studies relationships between numbers of meet- and join-irreducibles in finite lattices/posets.
status_evidence.claim: Related literature provides only partial bounds, not a determination of f(n).
